newsitem.title: TURKEY: France stalls on north Iraq no-fly zone talks.
newsitem.headline: France stalls on north Iraq no-fly zone talks.

text.p: Talks in Turkey on the future of U.S.-led air patrols over northern Iraq hit a snag on Wednesday when France disagreed on the details of more planned allied flights, Turkish officials said.
"France made it known this afternoon that it was not ready for an agreement on technical issues at the moment," a Turkish foreign ministry official told Reuters.
The mandate for joint U.S., British and French patrols of a no-fly zone that bans Baghdad's aircraft from northern Iraq is due to run out on December 31.
In Paris, a French foreign ministry spokesman said the United States and Turkey had decided to end on December 31 the "Provide Comfort" overflights as they had been conducted until now.
"French authorities will study the new conditions created by this decision and will make their position known at the right time," the spokesman said.
The source of the disagreement between Paris and its allies was not immediately clear.

The three allies have been shielding northern Iraq from any attack by Baghdad since hundreds of thousands of Iraqi Kurds fled to Turkey and Iran after a failed uprising at the end of the 1991 Gulf War.

France temporarily pulled out of the operation in September after U.S. cruise missile attacks against Iraq, when Washington backed one Kurdish faction against the other during internecine fighting in Kurdistan in August.
France pointedly refused to endorse the U.S. strikes, causing the most serious rift in the Gulf War coalition.
Paris, eager to help exploit Iraqi oil resources, has courted Baghdad's favour and pressed for an end to United Nations sanctions against Iraq.
If Paris and Washington failed to agree on future conduct in the area, it would be yet another in a series of disagreements between the two countries.

Recent quarrels have concerned European involvement in Arab-Israeli peace talks, control of NATO commands in southern Europe, French criticism of U.S. policy in Africa and a supposed snub of outgoing Secretary of State Warren Christopher by French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette.
The planes involved in the Iraqi operation fly out of the Incirlik air base in south Turkey.
Turkish MPs voted on Wednesday to give Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's government the power to authorise a continuation of the flights in January.
The French dispute is the latest blow to Washington's attempts to keep President Saddam Hussein's troops out of the mountainous north of Iraq.
The allied force's ground element in northern Iraq was scrapped after Saddam gained a foothold in the region in the inter-Kurdish fighting in late August.
The United States pulled out its aid, intelligence and military operations from the region and evacuated thousands of Iraqis affiliated with U.S. organisations.
